battle.title: The Hot Seat
battle.description: Turn behavioural questions into crisp Situation, Task, Action, Result stories.

questions.text: What does STAR stand for in behavioural interviews?
options: Skills, Training, Achievements, References
Situation, Task, Action, Result
Strategy, Tactics, Analysis, Review
Story, Timeline, Approach, Reflection
questions.explanation: STAR is Situation, Task, Action, Result, a structure for telling a concrete past example. The other lists sound professional but are not the method.

questions.text: "Tell me about a time you faced a conflict in a team project." Which opening is best?
options: I am a team player and I never really have conflicts
Teams always have conflicts, and in general I handle them well
In my final-year project we disagreed on the database a week before demo, and I had to resolve it
My teammate was lazy and did nothing, so I did everything
questions.answer: In my final-year project we disagreed on the database a week before demo, and I had to resolve it
questions.explanation: It sets a specific situation and your task in two sentences. Generic claims give no evidence, 'never any conflict' sounds evasive, and blaming a teammate is a red flag.

questions.text: In a STAR answer, where should most of your time go?
options: The Situation, so the interviewer has full background
The Action, focusing on what you personally did and why
The Task, repeating the goal several times
The Result, only if it was a big success
questions.answer: The Action, focusing on what you personally did and why
questions.explanation: Interviewers are assessing your behaviour, so Action carries the most weight. Long backstory is the classic way to run out of time before the part that matters.

questions.text: You describe an action in a group project. Which phrasing is strongest?
options: We did the backend and it kind of worked out
The team decided on the design and things went fine
Someone fixed the bug eventually
I wrote the API tests, found the failing endpoint, and fixed the null check, which unblocked the team
questions.answer: I wrote the API tests, found the failing endpoint, and fixed the null check, which unblocked the team
questions.explanation: Saying 'I' with concrete steps shows your own contribution. Constant 'we' or passive phrasing leaves the interviewer unable to tell what you actually did.

questions.text: "Tell me about a time you failed." Which ending is best?
options: State what went wrong, own your part, and describe what you changed afterwards, ideally with an outcome
Say the failure was mostly caused by unclear instructions from others
Pick a fake weakness like "I work too hard" so you look perfect
Skip the result and move to your next strength
questions.answer: State what went wrong, own your part, and describe what you changed afterwards, ideally with an outcome
questions.explanation: Failure questions test ownership and learning, so the Result should include the lesson and a changed behaviour. Blaming others or giving a disguised strength sounds evasive.
